passages.t: Have you forgotten? A word to the Judeans in Egypt
passages.happening:
The word comes to Jeremiah for all the Judeans living in Egypt, at Migdol, Tahpanhes and Memphis and in the land of Pathros (verse 1). They have seen the disaster God brought on Jerusalem and Judah's towns, now ruins (verse 2), because the people burned incense to other gods (verse 3). God sent his prophets again and again, telling them not to do the detestable thing he hates (verse 4), and they would not listen (verse 5). So his anger burned in Judah and Jerusalem (verse 6).

Why are they doing such harm to themselves now (verse 7)? Why provoke God by burning incense to other gods in Egypt (verse 8)? ‘Have you forgotten the wickedness of your fathers and of the kings of Judah and their wives, as well as the wickedness that you and your wives committed’ in Judah (verse 9)? To this day they have not humbled themselves (verse 10).

So God has set his face against them (verse 11). The remnant who chose to go to Egypt will meet their end there by sword and famine (verse 12), as Jerusalem did (verse 13), and none will return except a few fugitives (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Verse 1 names Judean communities across Egypt: Migdol and Tahpanhes in the eastern Delta, Memphis, the old capital near modern Cairo, and Pathros, the Hebrew name for Upper Egypt in the south. Judeans had settled there before Johanan's group arrived.

More than a century later, Aramaic papyri from the island of Elephantine in southern Egypt record a Jewish military colony there with its own temple to the God of Israel. Some of those papyri mention other gods alongside him, a mix of worship like the one this chapter condemns.

The question have you forgotten runs through the chapter. The people had just lived through the fall of Jerusalem, and they were already doing the same things again.
passages.later: Kings explains the fall in the same way: ‘the LORD did not turn away from the fury of His burning anger’ because of what Manasseh had done (2 Kings 23:26). Paul warns, ‘flee from idolatry’ (1 Corinthians 10:14).
passages.asks: God asks whether they have forgotten what led to the ruin they just lived through. Ask what lesson you learned in hardship and have already begun to forget. And ask what old habit you have carried with you into a new place.

passages.t: The Queen of Heaven: whose word will stand
passages.happening:
Then all the men who knew their wives burned incense to other gods, and all the women standing by, a great assembly, answer Jeremiah (verse 15). They will not listen to the word he has spoken in the LORD's name (verse 16). They will do everything they vowed: burn incense to the Queen of Heaven and pour out drink offerings to her, as they, their fathers, kings and officials did in Judah. ‘At that time we had plenty of food and good things’ (verse 17). ‘But from the time we stopped burning incense to the Queen of Heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her, we have lacked everything and have been perishing by sword and famine’ (verse 18). The women add that they made her cakes and offerings with their husbands' knowledge (verse 19).

Jeremiah answers that it was exactly that incense, in Judah's towns and Jerusalem's streets, that the LORD remembered (verse 21). He could no longer bear it, and the land became a desolation (verse 22). Because they burned incense and sinned against the LORD, this disaster came (verse 23).

Since they are determined to keep their vows, God swears by his great name that his name will no longer be invoked by anyone of Judah in Egypt (verses 25 and 26). A few will escape back to Judah, ‘and the whole remnant of Judah who went to dwell in the land of Egypt will know whose word will stand, Mine or theirs’ (verse 28). As a sign, God will hand Pharaoh Hophra over to his enemies, as he handed Zedekiah to Nebuchadnezzar (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
The Queen of Heaven was a goddess, probably the Mesopotamian Ishtar or a related goddess, linked with the evening star and fertility. Her worship was a household practice; chapter 7 described children gathering wood and women baking cakes for her.

The people's argument is not foolish, and the chapter lets it be heard in their own words. Life under Manasseh, who promoted other gods, had been fairly stable. The years after Josiah's reform about 622 BC brought Josiah's death, foreign rule and destruction. To them, the facts pointed one way: when they worshiped her, things went well.

Jeremiah answers that they have read the timeline too narrowly. The judgment fell because of generations of sin, including the long years before Josiah, and Josiah's reform had not changed the nation's heart.

Pharaoh Hophra, also called Apries, was overthrown in about 570 BC by his general Amasis after a military revolt. The chapter's last word makes his fall a sign.
passages.later: Jeremiah had seen the same worship in Jerusalem: ‘the women knead the dough to make cakes for the Queen of Heaven’ (Jeremiah 7:18). Habakkuk resolves to trust God even ‘Though the fig tree does not bud’ (Habakkuk 3:17).
passages.hard:
The people's argument seems based on real experience: things were better when they worshiped the Queen of Heaven. Why should they believe Jeremiah instead?

The argument is not foolish, and the chapter lets it be heard. Life under Manasseh was relatively stable, while the years after Josiah's reform brought his death, foreign rule and destruction. Jeremiah's reply is that they have read the timeline too narrowly: the judgment fell because of generations of gathered sin, including the long years of idolatry before Josiah, and Josiah's reform, though sincere, did not change the heart of the nation (3:10). Kings makes the same point (2 Kings 23:26).

The chapter does not pretend that faithfulness always brings quick prosperity. Its claim is that God's word, not short-term results, is the right measure of truth, a claim that asks for faith when the evidence seems to point the other way. It is no judgment on women; the men and women of the assembly answer together, and Jeremiah speaks to both.
passages.asks: The people judged God by how well things were going. Ask whether you measure God's truth by your circumstances. And ask what you would hold to if obedience seemed, for a time, to make things worse.
